warns.avocadoFridgeUnripe: An unripe avocado in the fridge ripens badly: when you cut it, parts of the flesh will be dark, black or stringy, with an unpleasant taste. Leave it at room temperature until it yields slightly to gentle pressure, then refrigerate it.
warns.coldStopsRipening: Cold stops unripe fruit from ripening and can leave it hard, flavorless and spotted. Keep it at room temperature until it ripens, then refrigerate it.
warns.tomatoFridge: Cold dulls a tomato's flavor and makes it mealy. Keep it at room temperature until it ripens.
warns.tomatoFridgeRipe: Cold takes flavor and firmness from tomatoes: refrigerate only if it's very ripe and you won't use it soon, and take it out 30 minutes before eating.
warns.potatoFridge: In the fridge, potato starch turns to sugar: they taste sweet and darken when fried. A cool, dark, ventilated place is better; if it's very hot and the fridge is all you have, use them soon.
warns.basilFridge: Cold turns basil leaves black: keep it in a glass of water at room temperature.

tips.freezeGeneral: Freeze in small portions in sealed bags or containers with the air pressed out, and write the date on them. Thaw in the fridge, not on the counter.
tips.doubt: The date is an estimate: if it smells off, has mold or feels slimy, throw it out even if it hasn't expired.
tips.dry: Keep it tightly closed in a cool, dry, dark place away from the stove and sunlight. If you see weevils, moths or mold, throw it out.
tips.riceCooked: Cooked rice goes in the fridge within 2 hours and should be eaten in 3 to 4 days: left out, it can make you sick even if it looks fine.
tips.spice: Keep away from heat, light and moisture (not above the stove). If they barely smell, they're not unsafe, just weaker. Paprika and chili powder keep their color better in the fridge.
tips.oil: Keep it closed in a dark, cool place away from the stove. If it smells rancid or like paint, throw it out.
tips.honey: It doesn't need the fridge: if it crystallizes, warm the jar in a water bath. Don't give honey to babies under 1 year old.
tips.chocolate: Keep it cool and dry. A white film from heat is harmless; it only changes the texture.
tips.flour: Keep it in an airtight container. Freezing it for 48 hours when you buy it prevents weevils; whole-grain flours and bran go rancid sooner, so they last longer in the freezer.
tips.nuts: Their fat goes rancid in the heat: in the fridge or freezer they last much longer. If they smell rancid or taste bitter, throw them out.
tips.driedFruit: Keep in an airtight jar away from heat. Once opened, they last longer in the fridge and stay softer.
tips.yeast: Once opened, close it well and keep it in the fridge or freezer. If it doesn't foam when proofed in warm sugar water, it's no good.
tips.coffee: Keep it sealed away from light and heat. To store it longer, freeze it in portions; in the fridge it picks up moisture and odors.
tips.panettone: Sealed, it keeps for months; once opened, wrap it well and eat it within 5 to 7 days, or freeze slices.
tips.pudding: The powder keeps for months in the pantry; once prepared, cover it in the fridge and eat it within 2 to 3 days.
tips.canned: Unopened, it keeps for years in a cool, dry place. Don't use cans that are bulging, rusted, leaking or badly dented. Once opened, move the contents to a covered container in the fridge (3 to 7 days).
tips.condiment: Unopened, keep it in the pantry. Once opened, refrigerate it and use a clean spoon so you don't contaminate it.
tips.creamySauce: Sauces with egg, cheese or cream (mayonnaise, huancaína) go in the fridge once opened or made and shouldn't sit out more than 2 hours (1 hour if it's very hot).
tips.stock: Unopened, keep it in the pantry; once opened, refrigerate it and use it within 4 days, or freeze it in cubes.
tips.juice: Unopened, it keeps in the pantry; once opened, refrigerate it and drink within 7 to 10 days. If it fizzes or smells fermented, throw it out.
tips.avocadoRipen: Leave it at room temperature until it yields slightly to gentle pressure (4 to 5 days). To speed it up, put it in a paper bag with a banana or an apple.
tips.avocadoRipeFridge: Once ripe, keep it in the fridge: it lasts about 3 to 4 more days.
tips.avocadoCut: If you cut it: squeeze lemon or lime over the flesh, leave the pit in and store it in an airtight container in the fridge (1 to 2 days).
tips.avocadoFreeze: Freeze only the pulp, mashed with a little lemon or lime juice; a whole avocado turns dark and mushy.
tips.ripeSoon: It's ripe: eat it within 1 to 2 days or move it to the fridge to last a few more days.
tips.bananaRipen: Don't refrigerate them while green: cold stops ripening. Keep them apart from other fruit, since they give off ethylene and make it ripen faster.
tips.bananaRipeFridge: Once ripe you can refrigerate them: the peel turns black but the flesh stays good for about 5 days.
tips.bananaFreeze: Peeled, whole or sliced, frozen bananas are great for smoothies, banana bread and homemade ice cream.
tips.plantain: Green ones are for tostones and chips; yellow with black spots for fried sweet plantains. Keep at room temperature; once ripe, refrigerate or freeze it peeled.
tips.plantainFreeze: Peel and cut it into pieces before freezing, in a bag with the air pressed out.
tips.mangoRipen: It ripens at room temperature (3 to 7 days): it's ready when it smells sweet near the stem and gives slightly when pressed. Once ripe, refrigerate it or freeze it in chunks.
tips.papayaRipen: It ripens at room temperature until the skin turns yellow and gives when pressed. Once ripe, refrigerate it for about 5 days or freeze it in cubes; green papaya is damaged by cold.
tips.pearRipen: It ripens at room temperature in 3 to 5 days; it softens from the inside out, so check the neck (near the stem): if it gives, it's ready. Once ripe, move it to the fridge.
tips.stoneRipen: Peaches and plums ripen at room temperature (faster in a paper bag). Once ripe, refrigerate them for 3 to 5 days. Chilled while unripe, they turn mealy.
tips.kiwiRipen: Hard kiwis keep for weeks in the fridge; to ripen them, leave them on the counter next to an apple or banana. They're ready when they give slightly.
tips.tomatoCounter: Keep them at room temperature, stem side up and out of direct sun, until they ripen.
tips.tomatoFreeze: For sauces: freeze them whole (the skin slips off when thawed) or as pulp.
tips.cherimoyaRipen: It ripens at room temperature in 2 to 5 days; it's ready when it gives to pressure. Once ripe, refrigerate it for 2 to 4 days. Dark skin is normal; freeze the seedless pulp.
tips.soursopRipen: It ripens in 2 to 4 days at room temperature; when it gives to pressure, refrigerate it or freeze the seedless pulp (up to 6 months).
tips.lucumaRipen: It ripens in 3 to 7 days at room temperature and is ready when it gives to pressure. Freeze the pitted pulp for ice cream and smoothies.
tips.apple: In the fridge's fruit drawer they last weeks. Keep them apart from other fruit and vegetables: they give off ethylene and speed up ripening.
tips.quince: Hard and very fragrant: keep it at room temperature, away from other fruit, until you use it; wrapped in the fridge it lasts longer.
tips.citrus: At room temperature they last about 1 week; in the fridge, 2 to 3. The juice or zest freezes well in cubes.
tips.coconut: Whole, it lasts a week at room temperature. Once opened, keep the flesh in the fridge (4 to 5 days) or freeze it grated (up to 6 months).
tips.melon: Whole, it lasts about 1 week at room temperature; cut, covered in the fridge for 3 to 4 days.
tips.pineapple: It doesn't ripen further once picked: choose one with a sweet smell. Whole, it keeps 2 to 3 days out; cut, 3 to 4 days in a covered container in the fridge.
tips.grapes: Store them unwashed in the fridge, in their perforated bag. Frozen, they make a cool snack.
tips.berries: Don't wash them until you're about to eat them: moisture spoils them. Store in a container lined with paper towel and remove any moldy ones so they don't spread.
tips.berriesFreeze: Freeze them spread on a tray first, then bag them so they don't clump.
tips.frozenFood: If it thawed in the fridge you can refreeze it; if it thawed in water or the microwave, cook it first. Never thaw food on the counter.
tips.exotic: Leave it at room temperature until it's ready (skin slightly soft or wrinkled), then refrigerate.
tips.pulpFreeze: The pulp freezes well in cubes, ready for juices and desserts.
tips.goldenberry: Leave them in their husk (the paper-like cover) until you use them and keep them somewhere cool and dry or in the fridge. Wash them right before eating.
tips.pomegranate: Whole, it lasts weeks; loose seeds keep about 5 days in the fridge or up to 9 months frozen.
tips.figs: They're very delicate: eat them within 1 to 3 days and don't wash them until you're about to eat them.
tips.potato: Keep them in a cool, dark, ventilated place (basket or paper bag), away from onions. If they turn green or sprout a lot, throw them out.
tips.sweetPotato: Keep in a cool, dry, dark place; not in the fridge: cold hardens the center and changes the flavor.
tips.yuca: It spoils quickly: use it within a few days. Peeled and cut, cover it with water in the fridge (3 days) or freeze it (up to 2 months). If it has black or gray streaks inside, throw it out.
tips.andean: Keep unwashed in a cool, dark, ventilated place. If it wrinkles or sprouts, use it soon.
tips.onion: Keep them dry and ventilated (mesh bag or basket), away from potatoes. Once cut, cover it in the fridge for 5 to 7 days, or freeze it chopped.
tips.garlic: Whole heads: a dry, ventilated, dark place. Peeled or chopped, they last a few days in the fridge (covered) or up to 3 months frozen.
tips.greenOnion: Wrap it in a damp paper towel in a bag in the fridge, or stand it roots-down in a glass of water. Chopped, it freezes well.
tips.ginger: Unpeeled and wrapped in paper towel in the fridge; or freeze it whole and grate what you need straight from the freezer.
tips.pepper: Keep them dry in a bag with paper towel in the least cold part of the fridge. They freeze whole or chopped (4 to 6 months), or as paste.
tips.freezeVeg: Blanch vegetables for 2 to 3 minutes in boiling water and cool them in ice water before freezing: they keep better color, flavor and texture.
tips.rootVeg: Cut off the leafy tops before storing (they draw moisture out of the root) and keep them in a bag in the vegetable drawer.
tips.stalks: Wrap it in foil or in a bag with paper towel in the fridge to keep it crisp.
tips.leafy: Don't wash them until you use them (or dry them very well) and store them with paper towel in a container or bag in the fridge: moisture wilts them.
tips.saladMix: Keep the bag closed; once opened, eat it within 2 to 3 days and pick out any slimy leaves.
tips.brassica: Store them unwashed in a perforated bag in the vegetable drawer and wash them just before cooking.
tips.crisper: Unwashed, in a perforated bag in the vegetable drawer; wash them just before using.
tips.eggplant: Eggplant is damaged by strong cold (spots and softening): keep it in the least cold part of the fridge and use it within a few days.
tips.sprouts: They're highly perishable: use them within 2 to 3 days, keep them cold and dry, and cook them well.
tips.mushrooms: Keep them in a paper bag (not plastic) in the fridge and don't wash them until you cook them.
tips.corn: Keep it in its husk in a perforated bag in the fridge: the sugar turns to starch quickly. To freeze, boil it 3 minutes, cool it and freeze it whole or off the cob.
tips.squash: Whole, it lasts weeks in a cool, dry place. Cut, covered in the fridge for 4 to 5 days; cooked and mashed it freezes up to 9 months.
tips.legumeFresh: They last longer in the pod. To freeze, blanch them for 2 minutes and cool them first.
tips.herbs: Stand the stems in a glass of water, cover the leaves with a bag and refrigerate; or wrap them in paper towel in a container. Chopped in oil or water, they freeze in cubes.
tips.eggs: Refrigerated, they last 3 to 5 weeks. Keep them in their carton on a shelf (not the door) and don't wash them before storing.
tips.eggsRoom: In the US eggs are sold washed and must always be refrigerated. Unwashed eggs keep a few days out, but in warm weather they spoil quickly: we recommend refrigerating them. Don't use cracked or dirty eggs.
tips.milk: Keep it on a shelf, not the door, and tightly closed. Once opened, drink it within 5 to 7 days (unopened UHT lasts months in the pantry). If you freeze it, leave room in the container: it expands.
tips.plantMilk: Unopened boxed milk keeps for months in the pantry; once opened, refrigerate it for 7 to 10 days. Shake before using.
tips.butter: Covered in the fridge so it doesn't absorb odors. For longer storage, freeze it in portions.
tips.cream: In the coldest part of the fridge and tightly closed; frozen, it's only good for cooking.
tips.cultured: Closed in the fridge. A little liquid on top is normal (stir it in); if there's mold, throw it out entirely.
tips.cheeseSoft: Fresh cheese is very perishable: always refrigerate it in a covered container; if it has sour-smelling whey or turns slimy, throw it out. Frozen, the texture changes but it's fine for cooking.
tips.cheeseHard: Wrap it loosely in wax paper or plastic wrap. If mold appears on a hard cheese, cut off at least 1 inch (2.5 cm) around it and keep using it; for soft or shredded cheese, throw it out.
tips.tofu: Once opened, keep it submerged in clean water in a covered container and change the water daily: it lasts 3 to 5 days. Frozen, it turns firmer and spongier.
tips.hummus: Covered in the fridge and served with a clean spoon: homemade lasts about 7 days.
tips.rawPoultry: Keep it in the coldest part, on the bottom shelf, in a container so it can't drip on other food. If you won't cook it within 1 or 2 days, freeze it. Don't wash it, and cook it to 165 °F (74 °C).
tips.rawMeat: On the bottom shelf, in the coldest part. Whole cuts: 3 to 5 days; freeze in portions with the date and thaw in the fridge.
tips.groundMeat: Ground and stew meat only keep 1 to 2 days in the fridge; otherwise freeze it in flat portions (they thaw faster) and cook it thoroughly.
tips.offal: Organ meats keep 1 to 2 days: if you won't use them, freeze them the same day.
tips.curedMeat: Once opened, cold cuts keep 3 to 5 days and bacon and sausages up to 1 week. Keep them covered and refrigerated; fresh (raw) chorizo is treated like raw meat.
tips.rawFish: Fresh fish: 1 to 2 days in the coldest part, well covered; otherwise freeze it the same day. It should smell like the sea, not like ammonia. For ceviche, use fish from the same day.
tips.shellfish: Live shellfish (mussels, clams, scallops) keep 1 to 2 days well chilled: discard open ones that don't close when tapped. Shrimp, squid and octopus also keep 1 to 2 days.
tips.bread: Bread dries out and goes stale faster in the fridge. If you won't eat it within 2 or 3 days, freeze it sliced and toast it straight from frozen. In humid climates, close it well to prevent mold.
tips.breadFreeze: Freeze it sliced in a sealed bag and take out only what you need.
tips.pastry: Anything with cream, dulce de leche or fresh fruit goes in the fridge (2 hours out at most). Dry baked goods keep better covered.
tips.freshPasta: Follow the date on the package; once opened, use it within 1 to 2 days. Frozen, it lasts about 2 months.
tips.leftovers: Refrigerate cooked food within 2 hours (1 hour if it's very hot), in shallow containers. It keeps 3 to 4 days; reheat it until steaming hot (165 °F / 74 °C).
